new_statements.quote: [p. 53] The P.P.P. stem in Tangale is formed by the low tone suffix -zi/-zi (-ji/-ji, -si/-si) which is added to the verb base. The final consonant of the verb base is being clipped if it is a voiced plosive (b or d). The stem has a low-low(-low) tone pattern although the first syllable usually carries a strong stress. [p. 27] There are two pertinent tone levels to be distinguished, low (unmarked) and high (á). Statistically most syllables in the language (probably more than 80%) are low (or, tonetically, mid). Thus, to a certain extent, the low tone may be taken as basic ('normal'), unmarked and the high tone as marked. Phonemic tone functions on the lexical as well as on the grammatical level.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tangale is described as a two-tone language (high vs. low, low unmarked and by far the more frequent; tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive). No general word-accent rule is given anywhere in the 'Phonological and prosodological remarks'. The only stress remark is stem-specific: in the passive perfect participle stem, which carries an all-low tone pattern, the first (stem) syllable 'usually carries a strong stress'. Read literally this is stem-initial stress noted for one verbal form, not a rule for the whole vocabulary.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'usually'; the remark is limited to the P.P.P. stem. Family-level surveys deny stress as a prosodic parameter in Chadic (Schuh 2017: 6, 89, held under gala1264); Hartmann & Zimmermann 2004: 227-229 find no prosodic prominence differences under focus and contrast Tangale with stress languages.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (verb stem in citation), in a grammatical sketch prefacing a dictionary of the Kaltungo (eastern) dialect. Quote is from the archive.org scanned layer of the Rosetta Project scan (checked against the page image text layer; suffix forms in the first sentence partly garbled in scanned, the deciding third sentence reads cleanly). Scan lacks pp. 29-30 (end of sec. 3.3.2), so a stress remark there cannot be excluded.
new_statements.identity_note: Jungraithmayr 1991 describes the Kaltungo (eastern) dialect of Tangale (with some Billiri items); Kidda 1985/1993 describes Shongom-Tangale; Hartmann & Zimmermann's consultant is from Kaltungo. Glottolog 5.1 places all under nucl1696 (no separate dialect languoids found on the page). The p. 53 stress remark is stem-specific (passive perfect participle), so the catalog entry should be flagged as a partial statement in a two-tone language rather than a general word-stress rule.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Phonological and prosodological remarks' (pp. 19-28) gives consonants, vowels, harmony, deletion and 3.3 Tone (p. 27: two tone levels, low unmarked and >80% of syllables, high marked; tone lexical and grammatical) but states no accent/stress rule. sources.note: FAMILY-LEVEL only: ch. 1 p. 6 '- stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter'; ch. 5 p. 89 'All Chadic languages are tone languages.. Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang.., but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties.' Tangale appears only in Bole-Tangale verb-tone discussion ((L)H pattern); no Tangale-specific stress remark.

sources.note: Treats Tangale (Kaltungo consultant) as a tone language and contrasts it with stress languages: p. 207 'it is standardly assumed that focus is generally marked by stress. The Chadic languages, however, exhibit a variety of different devices'; p. 227 'Tangale thus differs from stress languages, in which narrow V-focus is marked differently from narrow OBJ-focus by stress placement'; p. 229 in 42 recorded sentences 'no significant prosodic differences between V-, VP-, and OBJ-focus', pitch contours 'virtually identical'. No word-stress statement.
